paragraphs: An out-of-distribution detector needs both a score indicating how unfamiliar an input looks and a rule for deciding when that score warrants rejection. This paper focuses on the second component. Its central question is how to turn detection scores into decisions with explicit statistical guarantees, rather than concentrating only on improving the scoring function.

The authors frame detection as hypothesis testing and introduce a generalized Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, called g-BH, using empirical p-values. They prove that the procedure controls the false discovery rate at a level chosen in advance. This makes the decision rule itself a statistically governed part of the detector.

The paper also bounds the expected false positive rate using a tailed generalized Gaussian distribution family. Within that analysis, the false positive rate converges to zero in probability. Experiments on several detection benchmarks report improvements over traditional threshold rules. Together, these results connect practical decision quality with theoretical error control, while keeping the distribution-dependent false-positive result distinct from the broader false-discovery guarantee.
icml-2024-a-provable-decision-rule-for-o.tldr: A hypothesis-testing decision rule improves out-of-distribution detection while providing theoretical control of statistical errors.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how training a model to predict the next token can support complex computation. It develops a theoretical framework for autoregressive predictors, focusing on the contribution of the prediction process itself. The motivation is that substantial reasoning abilities appear in language models despite their seemingly simple training objective.

The central result shows that even linear next-token predictors, when trained on chain-of-thought data, can approximate any function efficiently computed by a Turing machine. The chain of intermediate tokens is an essential part of this statement. To study its role, the authors introduce length complexity: the number of intermediate tokens needed to approximate a target function.

The paper analyzes how this measure interacts with other notions of computational complexity. Experiments also find nontrivial text-generation and arithmetic performance in linear networks and shallow multilayer perceptrons. These findings support the importance of autoregressive training as a source of capability. They do not require attributing all language-model performance to a particular architecture, or imply that intermediate computation comes without a token-length cost.
icml-2024-auto-regressive-next-token-pre.tldr: Simple next-token predictors trained on chain-of-thought data can approximate efficiently computable functions, with intermediate-token length becoming a key complexity measure.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained language model to successive domains raises two connected problems: computation is expensive, and adaptation must account for more than the latest dataset. COPAL addresses these together through continual pruning. It uses the selection of model weights as a means of adaptation while avoiding resource-intensive fine-tuning or retraining.

The pruning decisions are guided by a sensitivity analysis. This analysis measures how well the model withstands perturbations introduced by a new dataset and identifies weights relevant across the datasets encountered so far. The history of adaptation therefore informs which parts of the model are retained, rather than treating each new domain as an isolated pruning problem.

Experiments across language models of different sizes report better results than the evaluated baselines, supporting the method's efficiency and adaptability. The contribution is a way to connect compression with ongoing domain adaptation: reducing model resources and responding to new data become parts of the same process. The stated evidence concerns that continual adaptation setting and the models included in the empirical evaluation.
icml-2024-copal-continual-pruning-in-lar.tldr: COPAL uses sensitivity-guided continual pruning to adapt language models across domains without resource-heavy fine-tuning or retraining.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce visually convincing images, but compression also requires a reconstruction to remain faithful to the original. A plausible-looking image can still contain substantial distortion. This paper combines diffusion reconstruction with an end-to-end decoder intended to correct that tension, improving perceived quality while controlling distortion to an extent.

The approach uses information available at the encoder, where the original image can still be examined. The authors theoretically analyze diffusion reconstruction from that perspective and introduce a convolutional decoder to provide a better approximation of the score function used in the diffusion process. Their design transmits privileged information extracted at the encoder to support the correction.

This makes the original image's availability during encoding part of how reconstruction is guided. Experiments report advantages in both distortion and perceptual quality over previous perceptual compression methods. The result supports combining generative reconstruction with an encoder-informed correction mechanism. Its distortion claim remains qualified: the abstract describes control to an extent, rather than an unrestricted guarantee of exact reconstruction.
icml-2024-correcting-diffusion-based-per.tldr: An encoder-informed correction decoder helps diffusion-based image compression improve visual quality while limiting reconstruction distortion.

paragraphs: Token-importance explanations claim to identify which words matter for a prediction, but a convincing explanation may misrepresent the model's behavior. One way to test it is to mask supposedly important tokens and check whether performance worsens. The problem is that masking can create inputs unlike those the model normally encounters, confusing the interpretation of the test.

This paper changes fine-tuning so that masked inputs belong to the model's intended input distribution. That makes masking a more suitable intervention for measuring explanation faithfulness. The approach builds this capability into the model, avoiding reliance on a separate proxy model for the measurement.

The authors apply the method to 16 datasets, use statistical tests to validate the distributional treatment of masking, and assess nine importance measures. Masking-based importance measures become consistently more faithful in their evaluation. Because faithfulness is also inexpensive to measure, explanations can be optimized against it. The contribution therefore connects model training, explanation evaluation, and explanation improvement within one approach.
icml-2024-faithfulness-measurable-masked.tldr: Fine-tuning with masking makes token-removal tests cheaper and more reliable for measuring and improving explanation faithfulness.

paragraphs: A world model helps a reinforcement-learning agent learn how its environment behaves. Training it typically involves modeling observations and rewards. This paper investigates what happens when either objective dominates, finding that the balance between them can substantially affect how efficiently the agent learns from experience.

Observation modeling supplies rich information but can demand more environmental detail than a limited-capacity model can capture. Reward modeling focuses on task-relevant dynamics, yet the authors find that it lacks sufficiently rich learning signals on its own for sample-efficient learning. HarmonyDream responds by automatically adjusting the coefficients of these two training losses, maintaining a changing balance as learning proceeds.

Experiments report absolute performance gains of 10%–69% when HarmonyDream is added to the base method on visual robotic tasks, alongside a new state-of-the-art result on Atari 100K. The findings suggest that better use of existing world-model objectives can unlock substantial performance improvements. The mechanism matters because it addresses how competing learning signals share model capacity, rather than simply asking the model to reconstruct more detail.
icml-2024-harmonydream-task-harmonizatio.tldr: HarmonyDream automatically balances observation and reward learning inside world models, improving sample-efficient reinforcement learning in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions described by many features when actions also consume limited resources. The learner must discover rewarding choices while staying within resource budgets, represented by knapsack constraints. The central opportunity is sparsity: useful structure can be concentrated in a relatively small portion of a high-dimensional representation.

The authors develop an online hard-thresholding estimator with optimal sparse-estimation performance. They combine it with a primal-dual method that assigns a separate dual variable to each resource constraint. An online learning algorithm updates these variables, allowing the decision process to account for how quickly each resource budget is being consumed.

The resulting method achieves sublinear regret with logarithmic dependence on feature dimension, improving the polynomial dependence of previous results. Regret measures the performance gap accumulated while learning, so sublinear growth means that gap grows more slowly than the decision horizon. The paper also treats the version without resource constraints, obtaining optimal regret in both data-poor and data-rich regimes. These results show how sparse estimation and budget management can be coordinated.
icml-2024-high-dimensional-linear-bandit.tldr: Combining online sparse estimation with resource-budget control yields bandit regret that depends only logarithmically on feature dimension.

paragraphs: Distributed training often splits data across workers that must communicate gradient information. This communication can become a bottleneck, and wireless links introduce noise as well as a need for efficiency. The paper targets a gap in compression methods: many assume noise-free transmission, while others deliver weak results on practical learning tasks.

LASER uses the low-rank structure present in gradients to compress and transmit them over noisy channels. Low-rank structure means the gradient information admits a more compact representation. Exploiting that structure connects the compression scheme to the information being communicated, while the method explicitly addresses transmission noise.

The authors establish theoretical guarantees similar to classical stochastic gradient descent and report consistent improvements over baselines across practical benchmarks. Their evaluations include computer vision and GPT language modeling. For language modeling over noisy channels, they report perplexity improvements of 50%–64% relative to their baselines. The findings support compression designed jointly around gradient structure and noisy communication, with both optimization theory and downstream model performance informing the assessment.
icml-2024-laser-linear-compression-in-wi.tldr: LASER exploits low-rank gradients to make distributed training effective over noisy wireless channels.

paragraphs: Scientific discovery involves proposing explanations, testing their consequences, and revising them using observations. This paper builds that division of work into Scientific Generative Agent, or SGA. Its motivation is that language models offer scientific knowledge and abstract reasoning, but have difficulty generating and grounding the observational feedback needed for physical discovery.

SGA combines a language model with simulation in a bilevel optimization framework. The language model handles discrete choices, such as the form of a physical equation or a molecular structure. The simulator supplies observational feedback and uses differentiability to optimize continuous quantities, such as physical parameters. These roles connect structural hypotheses with numerical testing and adjustment.

Experiments examine constitutive-law discovery and molecular design. The authors report effective discovery and novel solutions that differ from conventional human expectations while remaining coherent under analysis. The approach matters because it gives generated hypotheses a computational testing process. Its stated findings concern discovery through this combination of language-based reasoning and simulation, with each component contributing a different kind of optimization.
icml-2024-llm-and-simulation-as-bilevel-.tldr: SGA pairs language-model hypothesis generation with differentiable simulation to optimize scientific structures and their continuous parameters.

paragraphs: In simultaneous games, players choose actions without seeing what others are choosing at that moment. This complicates the transfer of planning and self-play methods successful in sequential games. Even when the game state is visible, other players may select different equilibria or act imperfectly, making their behavior an essential part of the decision problem.

Albatross addresses this by learning responses to agents with different levels of playing strength. It introduces a Smooth Best Response Logit Equilibrium and uses simulated self-play with temperature-based response optimization. The equilibrium concept is designed to support both cooperation and competition with players across levels of ability.

The evaluation covers cooperative and competitive simultaneous games with perfect information. In Battlesnake, Albatross exploits weak opponents in a way the evaluated AlphaZero approach does not. In Overcooked, it improves on the previous state of the art by 37.6%. These findings support explicitly accounting for bounded rationality when learning to interact with others, instead of relying only on expectations of optimal play.
icml-2024-mastering-zero-shot-interactio.tldr: Albatross models differing player strengths to improve cooperation and competition in simultaneous games.

paragraphs: Choosing a small set that reflects a larger population's diversity becomes difficult when items are described by categories. Categories lack a natural ordering, and the number of possible subsets creates a combinatorial search problem. This paper develops selection methods specifically for that setting, where existing selection techniques can be poorly suited.

The authors formulate subset selection as optimization under three diversity measures. They derive new bounds and develop exact solvers, providing ways to characterize and solve the optimization problem precisely. However, those exact methods have high computational costs, creating a practical barrier when searching for a diverse subset.

To address that barrier, the paper introduces two more computationally feasible methods using linear programming and submodular optimization. These methods retain approximation guarantees for the diversity measures, connecting efficiency with a quantified relationship to the optimization objective. Numerical comparisons illustrate their potential relative to existing methods. The contribution therefore includes both a mathematical treatment of categorical diversity and practical approaches for selecting representative sets without always paying the cost of exact optimization.
icml-2024-measures-of-diversity-and-spac.tldr: The paper develops diversity objectives and efficient approximation methods for selecting representative subsets of categorical data.

paragraphs: A high-dimensional linear model can fit noisy training labels exactly and still predict well, a phenomenon called benign overfitting. This behavior depends on conditions involving the source data's covariance and dimensionality. The paper asks what happens when such a model is transferred to inputs with a different distribution.

The authors prove non-asymptotic excess-risk bounds for benignly overfit linear interpolators under transfer learning. These bounds address finite settings rather than relying only on limiting behavior. Their analysis leads to a classification of beneficial and malignant covariate shifts, with the distinction depending on the degree of overparameterization.

Empirical studies illustrate both kinds of shift for linear interpolators using real image data. The authors also observe them for fully connected neural networks when input dimensionality exceeds the number of training examples. The result helps explain why a change in input distribution can have different consequences for models that fit their training data perfectly. The theoretical guarantees concern linear interpolators, while the neural-network findings provide a separate empirical extension.
icml-2024-minimum-norm-interpolation-und.tldr: Finite-sample theory identifies how covariate shifts can help or harm benignly overfit linear models depending on overparameterization.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines model updates from clients whose data remain distributed. Adding differential privacy introduces noise, but clients can have different privacy requirements, dataset sizes, and batch sizes. This paper shows that these differences produce varying noise levels in their updates, complicating how the server should combine them.

Robust-HDP estimates the actual noise in client updates and uses that information to reduce noise in the aggregate. This addresses a weakness of simple aggregation rules, such as weighting clients in proportion to their privacy parameters. A reported privacy parameter alone does not capture all the factors determining an update's noise level.

The method targets a setting where the server is not fully trusted. It also remains safe against clients that submit falsified privacy parameters, according to the abstract. Theoretical analysis and experiments on multiple datasets support improved utility and faster convergence. The contribution is to make heterogeneous private aggregation responsive to estimated update noise, connecting the privacy setting to the quality of the shared learning signal.
icml-2024-noise-aware-algorithm-for-hete.tldr: Robust-HDP estimates client-update noise to improve federated learning with heterogeneous privacy requirements and data sizes.

paragraphs: Probabilistic neurosymbolic models combine neural networks with logical reasoning under uncertainty. Training them by gradient descent requires differentiating through that reasoning process. This paper studies the computational difficulty of obtaining those gradients, making the learning calculation itself the central object of analysis.

The authors prove that approximating the gradients is intractable in general, but becomes tractable during training. They also introduce WeightME, an unbiased estimator based on model sampling. Under mild assumptions, it provides probabilistic guarantees on gradient approximation using a logarithmic number of calls to a SAT solver. The assumptions qualify this computational guarantee.

Experiments investigate whether gradient guarantees matter for optimization in practice. Existing biased approximations struggle even in cases where exact solving remains feasible. This connects the theoretical analysis to a practical concern: an approximation that is easier to compute may still provide a poor training signal. WeightME offers a route toward gradients with explicit statistical properties, while the hardness result explains why unrestricted gradient approximation is a difficult starting point.
icml-2024-on-the-hardness-of-probabilist.tldr: The paper analyzes neurosymbolic gradient complexity and introduces an unbiased estimator with conditional probabilistic guarantees.

paragraphs: This position paper advocates automated scientific discovery using datasets already available to a system. Its proposed scope covers both searching for hypotheses and checking them against those datasets, without collecting new data or conducting physical experiments. Large generative models are presented as a promising component of that broader discovery process.

The authors describe desired properties of an ideal system and introduce DataVoyager, a GPT-4-based proof of concept. It demonstrates several of those properties while exposing limitations that motivate further machine-learning research. The demonstration supports progress toward automated discovery, rather than establishing that a complete, reliable system has already been achieved.

The paper argues that current generative-model capabilities alone make accurate, reliable, and robust end-to-end discovery challenging. It therefore advocates dependable tool integration and active user moderation through feedback. These recommendations make verification and human guidance part of the proposed research direction. The central contribution is an agenda for turning generative models into useful participants in efficient, reproducible discovery grounded in existing data.
icml-2024-position-data-driven-discovery.tldr: This position paper advocates generative-model discovery systems grounded in existing datasets, dependable tools, and active user feedback.

paragraphs: Feature attribution aims to locate the parts of an input relevant to classification. That localization is especially useful when scientific or biomedical interpretation depends on identifying specific patterns. The paper argues that existing methods for explaining complete classifiers can localize imprecisely and face computational difficulties with small samples and high-dimensional data.

Prospector heads provide an efficient, interpretable alternative that the authors describe as applicable to any encoder and data modality. The approach is evaluated across text sequences, pathology images, and graphs representing protein structures. This range tests whether the attribution framework can operate across substantially different kinds of input.

The reported improvement over baseline attribution methods reaches 26.3 points in mean localization AUPRC, a measure used here to assess localization quality. The authors also demonstrate improved interpretation and discovery of patterns associated with particular classes. These findings make the contribution more specific than producing persuasive explanations: it aims to identify relevant input regions accurately enough to support analysis across complex scientific data.
icml-2024-prospector-heads-generalized-f.tldr: Prospector heads improve localization of class-relevant input regions across text, pathology images, and protein graphs.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent needs to discover useful parts of its environment before it can reliably exploit them. That search becomes difficult when the state space is high-dimensional. Random Latent Exploration, or RLE, addresses this by changing the rewards used during training to encourage exploration.

RLE adds structured random rewards to the original task rewards in certain randomly selected states. It combines ideas from exploration bonuses and randomized value functions. The additional rewards give the agent exploratory incentives alongside the task's existing objective, making reward perturbation the mechanism through which randomness influences behavior.

The authors describe the method as straightforward to implement and evaluate it on Atari and IsaacGym. They report higher overall scores across the evaluated tasks than competing approaches, including action-noise exploration and randomized value functions. These findings support the practical usefulness of structured random rewards in the tested settings. The contribution is a relatively direct way to combine two established exploration ideas within the reward signal used for learning.
icml-2024-random-latent-exploration-for-.tldr: Random Latent Exploration adds structured random rewards during training to improve exploration and overall benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Sparse or delayed rewards leave a reinforcement-learning agent with little immediate guidance about whether its actions are useful. This paper introduces a second agent whose job is to provide auxiliary rewards. The policy agent learns how to act, while the reward agent learns signals intended to make that learning process more informative.

The framework learns these signals without expert knowledge or manually designed reward functions. Its reward restructuring captures information oriented toward future outcomes. The authors report that this improves both sample efficiency and convergence stability, connecting the additional feedback to how quickly and consistently the policy learns.

The auxiliary rewards also play different roles over training: they encourage environmental exploration early and support exploitation of the learned policy later. The authors describe this as a self-adaptive balance. Evaluations on continuous-control tasks with sparse and delayed rewards report robustness and advantages over existing methods. The contribution is therefore a learned partnership between behavior selection and reward generation, designed to provide useful guidance as the policy's needs change.
icml-2024-reward-shaping-for-reinforceme.tldr: A learned reward agent supplies auxiliary feedback that helps a policy agent learn from sparse and delayed rewards.

paragraphs: Representation learning must organize examples so that their learned features support useful distinctions between classes. SCoRe addresses inter-class bias and variation within classes through a combinatorial view of the training objective. It introduces losses built from submodular information measures defined over sets.

The framework develops two formulations based on Total Information and Total Correlation. These are designed to reduce both intra-class variance and inter-class bias. Several established objectives, including supervised contrastive loss, orthogonal projection loss, and N-pairs loss, emerge as instances of SCoRe. This unifies familiar losses while providing a basis for constructing new ones.

The new objectives also naturally model class imbalance. Reported classification improvements reach 7.6% across CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-100-LT, and MedMNIST, with a 2.1% improvement on ImageNet-LT. The abstract additionally reports object-detection improvements reaching 19.4% on IDD and LVIS. These empirical results support the value of treating class structure and imbalance through set-based objectives, alongside the framework's contribution in connecting previously separate loss formulations.
icml-2024-score-submodular-combinatorial.tldr: SCoRe unifies familiar representation-learning losses and introduces set-based objectives that address class variation, bias, and imbalance.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning requires an agent to learn successive tasks while preserving useful earlier behavior. This paper introduces a modular neural architecture that can grow as tasks arrive. Its structure is designed to avoid catastrophic forgetting and interference while allowing previous policies to contribute to new learning.

Each module can selectively combine earlier policies with its own internal policy. That makes reuse a choice within the architecture: existing behavior can help solve the current task alongside newly learned behavior. The authors report that this composition accelerates learning, connecting retained knowledge to the agent's ability to adapt.

The paper also shows that parameter count grows linearly with the number of tasks while preserving plasticity, the capacity to learn new behavior. Experiments on continuous-control and visual benchmarks report stronger knowledge transfer and performance than alternative methods. The contribution brings retention, reuse, and growth into one architecture. Its scalability result concerns linear growth rather than a fixed model size, making the resource cost of accumulating tasks an explicit part of the design.
icml-2024-self-composing-policies-for-sc.tldr: A growing modular policy architecture reuses earlier policies, avoids forgetting, and scales linearly with the number of tasks.

paragraphs: Embedding services turn text into vectors useful for downstream tasks, but sending text directly to a server creates privacy concerns. Split-N-Denoise addresses this during language-model inference by dividing computation between the client and server. The design places the token-embedding layer on the client at a stated minimal computational cost.

The client adds noise to those embeddings before transmission. After the server processes the perturbed representations, the client receives output embeddings and denoises them for downstream use. This pairs local privacy protection with a recovery step intended to preserve useful semantic information. The framework requires no changes to the language model's parameters.

Experiments cover multiple language-model architectures and varied downstream tasks. At the same privacy budget, the authors report average performance improvements exceeding 10% over baselines. The finding concerns the privacy–utility tradeoff: useful task performance improves while the comparison holds the privacy budget fixed. The approach makes both the point of noise introduction and the treatment of noisy outputs part of the inference design.
icml-2024-split-and-denoise-protect-larg.tldr: Split-N-Denoise adds privacy noise to client-side embeddings and denoises returned representations to improve utility at a fixed privacy budget.

paragraphs: Vision-language models need to connect complete images with sentences and also align their finer details. Contrastive Captioners combine global image-text matching with image-to-text generation. This paper identifies an asymmetry at the local level: generating text from visual features does not also impose a corresponding text-to-image reconstruction task.

SyCoCa adds text-guided masked image modeling to establish local interactions in both directions. Text helps reconstruct image content, while visual information helps predict text. Together with global alignment, these objectives encourage connections between the modalities at more than one level of detail.

Not every image region is useful for this interaction, because local content can be cluttered or unrelated to its description. An attentive masking strategy selects effective image patches for the task. Experiments support the approach across image-text retrieval, captioning, visual question answering, and zero-shot and fine-tuned classification. The contribution is a more symmetric training design whose local reconstruction signals focus on image content relevant to the cross-modal interaction.
icml-2024-sycoca-symmetrizing-contrastiv.tldr: SyCoCa adds text-guided image reconstruction and attentive masking to strengthen bidirectional local image-text alignment.

paragraphs: Diffusion models built with UNets use skip connections to pass information between encoder and decoder blocks. These shortcuts help training, but the paper argues they can also limit transformation complexity. That matters especially when generation uses fewer sampling steps, requiring the network to perform a more demanding transformation from noise toward the image distribution.

Skip-Tuning adjusts those connections without additional training. The authors report an FID of 1.75 for pretrained EDM on ImageNet 64 using 19 network function evaluations. Improvements persist with more sampling steps: at 39 evaluations, the reported FID is 1.57, slightly better than the cited best EDM-2 result of 1.58.

Exploratory experiments examine why the adjustment helps. Pixel-space score-matching losses increase, while feature-space losses decrease, particularly at intermediate noise levels. Those levels also correspond to the range contributing most effectively to image-quality improvements. The observations suggest that better sampling quality can accompany worse pixel-space loss, making the representation used to assess prediction errors relevant to understanding the tuning effect.
icml-2024-the-surprising-effectiveness-o.tldr: Training-free tuning of UNet skip connections improves diffusion image generation, with gains associated with lower feature-space prediction losses.

paragraphs: Large language-model benchmarks can contain tens of thousands of examples, making repeated evaluation expensive. This paper investigates how to estimate benchmark performance using far fewer model evaluations. Its focus is preserving useful information about the original evaluation result while reducing the amount of testing required.

For MMLU, a multiple-choice question-answering benchmark with roughly 14,000 examples, the authors show that 100 curated examples are sufficient for an accurate performance estimate in their study. The selection is important to the claim: the result concerns a curated small set, rather than establishing that any 100 questions would work.

The paper releases evaluation tools and compact versions of the Open LLM Leaderboard, MMLU, HELM, and AlpacaEval 2.0. Its empirical analysis finds that these resources reliably and efficiently reproduce the original evaluation results. This suggests a practical way to reduce evaluation costs when full benchmark runs are burdensome. The contribution is both an investigation of reduced evaluation and a collection of usable small benchmarks supported by empirical comparisons.
icml-2024-tinybenchmarks-evaluating-llms.tldr: Curated tiny benchmarks can estimate full language-model evaluation results using far fewer examples.

paragraphs: Simplicial data represents higher-order relationships that go beyond ordinary graph connections. Neural models for this data can be costly to train and dependent on labels for a specific task. This paper introduces simplicial scattering networks, or SSNs, to extract task-independent representations without labels or learned parameters.

The method constructs scattering transforms from random-walk matrices associated with different adjacencies in a simplicial complex. These transforms form a deep bank of filters that captures high-frequency information across multiple scales. The design provides a structured way to extract features while avoiding the parameter-training process of a conventional neural representation model.

The authors establish permutation invariance, robustness to perturbations, and expressivity properties. They also prove that incorporating higher-order information improves robustness. Empirical evaluations report computational efficiency and stronger performance than existing simplicial or graph neural models across many tasks, including classification, trajectory prediction, and simplex prediction. These findings support fixed, mathematically structured feature extraction as a useful approach to higher-order data, with theoretical properties complementing the task evaluations.
icml-2024-unsupervised-parameter-free-si.tldr: Simplicial scattering networks extract label-free, parameter-free higher-order features with theoretical robustness properties and strong empirical performance.
